title: Fundamental Theorems And Distribution Theory
notes: Open by telling the audience that this chapter is the bridge between circular descriptions and usable asymptotic machinery. The page span is printed pages 57 through 82, PDF pages 74 through 99, and the lecture will treat the circle as both a Fourier object and a random-walk endpoint.

title: The Chapter Arc
notes: Use the four station route to prevent the lecture from becoming a list of unrelated facts. Integer harmonics identify circular laws, resultants translate samples into planar vectors, limit theorems explain when tangent normal coordinates are legal, and high concentration gives chi-square approximations with a visible geometric split.

title: A Circular Law Is A Harmonic Fingerprint
notes: Emphasize the difference from the line. The natural frequency grid is the set of integers, so a distribution is probed by a countable coefficient sequence. The picture shows that magnitude records how much harmonic structure survives while phase records the angular alignment of that structure.

title: Operations Become Coefficient Algebra
notes: Present this as the reason characteristic functions are more than a diagnostic plot. Rotation multiplies each harmonic by a phase factor, convolution multiplies matching coefficients, and conjugate symmetry remembers that the original measure is real. These rules are the computational form of the fundamental theorems.

title: Model Fingerprints Look Different
notes: Walk through the strip from left to right. Uniformity kills every nonzero harmonic, a lattice law keeps exact spikes, a cardioid only perturbs the first harmonic, wrapped normal coefficients decay quadratically in frequency, and von Mises coefficients decay through Bessel ratios. The goal is recognition, not memorization.

title: Resultants Turn Angles Into A Random Walk
notes: Move from distribution theory to sample geometry. Each observation contributes a unit vector, and the endpoint contains both the mean direction and the resultant length. Under isotropy the direction of the endpoint is not informative, but the radius remains a statistic with a nontrivial distribution.

title: Uniform Resultants Have A Rayleigh Scale
notes: The key normalization is not the raw length but two n times the squared mean resultant length. For many independent uniform angles, the endpoint coordinates behave like a planar normal, so the squared radius approaches chi-square with two degrees of freedom. Stress that small samples still keep exact circular geometry.

title: The Mean Direction Is A Derived Coordinate
notes: This slide is about a common failure mode. The planar average has a central limit theorem even when its endpoint lies near the origin, but the angle coordinate is unstable at zero length. Tangent normal approximations require a nonzero population resultant so the atan map can be linearized.

title: Planar CLT First, Tangent CLT Second
notes: State the order of operations clearly. First apply the multivariate central limit theorem to the cosine-sine average. Then project the resulting ellipse onto the tangent line at the population mean direction. This is why the angular variance is a delta-method quantity rather than a primitive scalar variance.

title: Von Mises Gives Explicit Variance Pieces
notes: For the von Mises model, Bessel ratios provide concrete covariance entries for the cosine and sine coordinates after rotating the mean to zero. The perpendicular variance controls mean-direction error, while the parallel variance controls resultant-length fluctuation. Keeping the two axes separate avoids overusing a one-dimensional normal story.

title: High Concentration Makes The Circle Locally Flat
notes: When concentration is large, most mass lives in a narrow arc near the mean direction. Rescaling angular deviations by the square root of kappa turns the arc into an approximately normal coordinate. The visual target is the transition from curved circle geometry to an almost straight tangent calculation.

title: Quadratic Scatter Splits Into Two Pieces
notes: Use the brace diagram to connect the approximation to ordinary normal sums of squares. The total centered scatter around the true direction separates into variation around the fitted mean and movement of the fitted mean itself. The corrected concentration gamma keeps the approximation accurate deeper into finite samples.

title: Approximation Regimes Are Not Interchangeable
notes: This is the applied warning slide. Increasing n helps the uniform random-walk chi-square limit, while increasing kappa helps the local normal and high-concentration chi-square limits. A procedure can be asymptotically correct and still be a poor numerical approximation for the regime in front of us.

title: A Diagnostic Workflow
notes: Frame the workflow as a reproducible habit. Identify whether the statistic is radial, angular, or high-concentration quadratic; simulate at the planned sample size and concentration; compare against the reference law; and only then decide whether the approximation is accurate enough for inference.

title: Common Mistakes To Catch Early
notes: Use this slide to slow down before the recap. Most mistakes come from treating angles as line variables, applying an angle normal approximation when the resultant is near zero, or borrowing a high-concentration formula in a diffuse sample. Each mistake has a visible diagnostic in the preceding slides.

title: What Survives The Chapter
notes: Close by tying the four tools together. Characteristic functions identify and manipulate circular laws; resultants turn samples into planar endpoints; circular limit theorems explain which coordinates can be approximated normally; and high concentration converts local angular scatter into chi-square pieces. The notebook path records the executable version of this lecture.
